chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Princess Mary was not in Moscow and out of danger, as Prince Andrew supposed.

After Alpatych's return from Smolensk, the old prince seemed suddenly to wake from a dream. He ordered the militiamen to be called up from the villages and armed, and wrote a letter to the commander in chief informing him that he had resolved to remain at Bald Hills to the last and defend it, where one of Russia's oldest generals would be captured or killed, leaving it to the commander in chief's discretion whether to take measures for Bald Hills' defense. He announced to his household that he would stay.

But while remaining himself, he ordered the departure of the princess and Dessalles with the little prince to Bogucharovo and then to Moscow. Princess Mary, alarmed by her father's feverish, sleepless activity after his previous apathy, could not bring herself to leave him alone and for the first time in her life dared to disobey him. She refused to go, and her father's fury crashed down on her like a terrible storm. He repeated every injustice he had ever done her. Trying to prove her guilty, he told her she had worn him out, had caused his quarrel with his son, had harbored nasty suspicions of him, and had made it her life's purpose to poison his existence. He drove her from his study, telling her that if she didn't leave it made no difference to him. He declared he did not wish to remember her existence and warned her not to dare let him see her. The fact that he did not, as she had feared, order her to be taken away by force, but only told her not to let him see her, cheered Princess Mary. She knew it proved that in the depth of his soul he was glad she was staying and had not left.

The morning after little Nicholas had departed, the old prince put on his full dress uniform and prepared to visit the commander in chief. His carriage was already at the door. Princess Mary saw him walk out of the house in his uniform with all his decorations and go down the garden to review his armed peasants and household servants. She sat by the window listening to his voice coming from the garden. Suddenly several men came running up the avenue with frightened faces.

Princess Mary ran out to the porch, down the flower-bordered path, and into the avenue. A large crowd of militiamen and servants were moving toward her, and in their midst several men were supporting by the arms and dragging along a little old man in a uniform and decorations. She ran up to him and, in the play of sunlight that fell in small round spots through the shade of the lime trees, could not be sure what change there was in his face. All she could see was that his former stern and determined expression had given way to one of timidity and helplessness. On seeing his daughter, he moved his helpless lips and made a hoarse sound. It was impossible to make out what he wanted. He was lifted up, carried to his study, and laid on the very couch he had so dreaded lately.
The doctor, who was fetched that same night, bled him and said the prince had had a stroke paralyzing his right side.
It was becoming more and more dangerous to remain at Bald Hills, and the next day they moved the prince to Bogucharovo, the doctor accompanying him.
By the time they reached Bogucharovo, Dessalles and the little prince had already left for Moscow.

For three weeks the old prince lay stricken with paralysis in the new house Prince Andrew had built at Bogucharovo, always in the same condition, getting neither better nor worse. He was unconscious and lay like a distorted corpse. He muttered unceasingly, his eyebrows and lips twitching, and it was impossible to tell whether he understood what was going on around him or not. One thing was certain—he was suffering and wanted to say something. But what it was, no one could tell: it might be some whim of a sick, half-mad old man, or it might relate to public affairs, or possibly to family concerns.

The doctor said this restlessness was meaningless and due to physical causes; but Princess Mary believed he was trying to tell her something, and the fact that her presence always increased his agitation confirmed her belief.

He was clearly suffering both physically and mentally. There was no hope of recovery. It was impossible for him to travel, and it would not do to let him die on the road. "Would it not be better if the end came—the very end?" Princess Mary sometimes thought. Night and day, barely sleeping at all, she watched him and, terrible to say, often watched him not hoping to find signs of improvement but wishing to spot symptoms that the end was approaching.

Strange as it was for her to admit this feeling, it was there. And what seemed still more terrible was that since her father's illness began (perhaps even earlier, when she stayed with him expecting something to happen), all the personal desires and hopes that had been forgotten or dormant within her had awakened. Thoughts that hadn't entered her mind for years—thoughts of a life free from the fear of her father, and even the possibility of love and family happiness—floated continually through her imagination like temptations of the devil. Push them aside as she might, questions kept recurring about how she would arrange her life now, after this. These were temptations of the devil, and Princess Mary knew it. She knew that the only weapon against him was prayer, and she tried to pray. She assumed the posture of prayer, looked at the icons, repeated the words of a prayer, but she could not pray. She felt that a different world had taken hold of her—a world of strenuous and free activity, entirely opposed to the spiritual world in which she had previously been confined and in which her greatest comfort had been prayer. She could not pray, could not weep, and worldly cares possessed her.
It was becoming dangerous to stay at Bogucharovo. News of the French approach came from all sides, and in one village ten miles from Bogucharovo, a homestead had been looted by French marauders.

The doctor insisted on the necessity of moving the prince; the provincial Marshal of the Nobility sent an official to Princess Mary to urge her to get away as quickly as possible; and the police chief, having come to Bogucharovo, urged the same thing, saying the French were only about twenty-five miles away, that French proclamations were circulating in the villages, and that if the princess did not take her father away before the fifteenth, he could not answer for the consequences.

The princess decided to leave on the fifteenth. The cares of preparation and giving orders, for which everyone came to her, occupied her all day. She spent the night of the fourteenth as usual, without undressing, in the room next to the one where the prince lay. Several times, waking up, she heard his groans and muttering, the creaking of his bed, and the steps of Tikhon and the doctor as they turned him over. Several times she listened at the door, and it seemed to her that his muttering was louder than usual and that they were turning him more often. She could not sleep, and several times went to the door and listened, wanting to go in but unable to decide. Though he didn't speak, Princess Mary saw and knew how unwelcome every sign of worry on his account was to him. She had noticed how he turned away from the look she sometimes fixed on him involuntarily. She knew that going in during the night at an unusual hour would irritate him.

But never had she felt so sad for him or so afraid of losing him. She recalled her entire life with him, and in every word and act found an expression of his love for her. Occasionally, among these memories, temptations of the devil would surge into her imagination: thoughts of how things would be after his death, and how her new, free life would be arranged. But she drove these thoughts away with disgust. Toward morning he became quiet and she fell asleep.

She woke late. The honesty that often comes with waking showed her clearly what mattered most about her father's illness. On waking, she listened to what was happening behind the door and, hearing him groan, said to herself with a sigh that things were still the same.
"But what could have happened? What did I want? I want his death!" she cried with self-loathing.
She washed, dressed, said her prayers, and went out to the porch. Carriages without horses stood in front of it; things were being packed into the vehicles.

It was a warm, gray morning. Princess Mary stopped at the porch, still horrified by her own spiritual baseness, trying to collect her thoughts before going in to her father. The doctor came downstairs and came out to her.
"He's a little better today," he said. "I was looking for you. You can make out something of what he's saying. His head is clearer. Come in—he's asking for you..."

Princess Mary's heart beat so hard at this news that she turned pale and leaned against the wall to keep from falling. To see him, talk to him, to feel his eyes on her now that her whole soul was overflowing with those terrible, wicked temptations, was a torment of joy and terror.
"Come," said the doctor.

Princess Mary entered her father's room and went to his bed. He was lying on his back, propped up high, and his small bony hands with their knotted purple veins lay on the quilt; his left eye gazed straight ahead, his right eye was askew, and his brows and lips were motionless. He seemed altogether so thin, small, and pitiful. His face seemed to have shriveled or melted; his features had grown smaller. Princess Mary went up and kissed his hand. His left hand pressed hers so tightly that she understood he had been waiting for her for a long time. He twitched her hand, and his brows and lips quivered angrily.

She looked at him in dismay, trying to guess what he wanted. When she shifted position so that his left eye could see her face, he calmed down, not taking his eyes off her for several seconds. Then his lips and tongue moved, sounds came, and he began to speak, gazing timidly and imploringly at her, obviously afraid she might not understand.

Straining every faculty, Princess Mary looked at him. The clumsy efforts with which he moved his tongue made her lower her eyes and struggle to hold back the sobs rising in her throat. He said something, repeating the same words several times. She couldn't understand them, but tried to guess and repeated back what she thought he was saying.
"Mmm... ar... ate... ate..." he repeated several times.
It was quite impossible to understand these sounds. The doctor thought he had guessed, and asked: "Mary, are you afraid?" The prince shook his head, and repeated the same sounds again.
"My mind, my mind aches?" asked Princess Mary.
He made a mumbling sound in confirmation, took her hand, and began pressing it to different parts of his chest as if trying to find the right place for it.
"Always thoughts... about you... thoughts..." he then said, much more clearly than before, now that he was sure of being understood.
Princess Mary pressed her head against his hand, trying to hide her sobs and tears.
He moved his hand over her hair.
"I have been calling you all night..." he managed to say.
"If only I had known..." she said through her tears. "I was afraid to come in."
He pressed her hand.
"Weren't you sleeping?"
"No, I didn't sleep," said Princess Mary, shaking her head.
Unconsciously imitating her father, she now tried to express herself as he did—as much as possible by gestures—and her tongue too seemed to move with difficulty.

"Dear one... dearest..." Princess Mary couldn't quite make out what he had said, but from his look it was clear he had spoken a tender, loving word such as he had never used with her before. "Why didn't you come in?"
"And I was wishing for his death!" thought Princess Mary.
He was silent for a while.

"Thank you... daughter dear... for everything, for everything... forgive... thank you!... forgive!... thank you!" and tears began to flow from his eyes. "Call Andrew!" he said suddenly, and a childish, timid expression of doubt showed on his face.
He seemed to know himself that his request was meaningless. So at least it seemed to Princess Mary.
"I have a letter from him," she replied.
He looked at her with timid surprise.
"Where is he?"
"He's with the army, Father, at Smolensk."
He closed his eyes and was silent for a long time. Then, as if in answer to his own doubts and to confirm that he now understood and remembered everything, he nodded and reopened his eyes.
"Yes," he said softly and distinctly. "Russia is ruined. They've destroyed her."
And he began to sob, and tears again flowed from his eyes. Princess Mary could no longer hold back and wept as she gazed at his face.
He closed his eyes again. His sobs ceased. He pointed to his eyes, and Tikhon, understanding him, wiped away the tears.

Then he opened his eyes again and said something that none of them could understand for a long time, until at last Tikhon grasped it and repeated it. Princess Mary had been searching for the meaning of his words in the mood of what he had just been saying. She thought he was speaking of Russia, or Prince Andrew, of herself, of his grandson, or of his own death, and so she couldn't guess.
"Put on your white dress. I like it," was what he said.

Having understood this, Princess Mary sobbed even harder, and the doctor, taking her arm, led her out to the veranda, trying to soothe her and persuade her to prepare for the journey. After she had left the room, the prince began speaking again about his son, about the war, about the Emperor, angrily twitching his brows and raising his hoarse voice, and then he had a second and final stroke.

Princess Mary stayed on the veranda. The day had cleared; it was hot and sunny. She could understand nothing, think of nothing, feel nothing except passionate love for her father—a love such as she thought she had never felt until that moment. She ran out sobbing into the garden and as far as the pond, along the avenue of young lime trees Prince Andrew had planted.

"Yes... I... I... I wished for his death! Yes, I wanted it to end sooner... I wanted peace... And what will become of me? What use will peace be when he is gone?" Princess Mary murmured, pacing the garden with hurried steps and pressing her hands to her heaving chest.

When she had walked around the whole garden and come back to the house, she saw Mademoiselle Bourienne—who had remained at Bogucharovo and did not wish to leave—coming toward her with a stranger. This was the Marshal of the Nobility for the district, who had come in person to impress upon the princess the urgency of leaving immediately. Princess Mary listened without understanding him; she led him into the house, offered him lunch, and sat down with him. Then, excusing herself, she went to the door of the old prince's room. The doctor came out with an agitated face and said she couldn't go in.
"Go away, Princess! Go away... go away!"

She went back to the garden and sat down on the grass at the foot of the slope by the pond, where no one could see her. She didn't know how long she had been there when she was roused by the sound of a woman's footsteps hurrying along the path. She looked up. It was Dunyasha, her maid, who had obviously been looking for her and stopped short in alarm on seeing her mistress.
"Please come, Princess... The Prince," said Dunyasha in a breaking voice.
"Right away, I'm coming, I'm coming!" replied the princess hurriedly, not giving Dunyasha time to finish, and trying not to look at the girl, she ran toward the house.
"Princess, it is God's will! You must be prepared for everything," said the Marshal, meeting her at the door.
"Leave me alone; it's not true!" she cried angrily.

The doctor tried to stop her. She pushed him aside and ran to her father's door. "Why are these people with frightened faces blocking my way? I don't need any of them! And what are they doing here?" she thought. She opened the door and the bright daylight in that previously darkened room startled her. In the room were her nurse and other women. They all drew back from the bed, making way for her. He was still lying on the bed as before, but the stern expression on his quiet face made Princess Mary stop short at the threshold.

"No, he's not dead—it's impossible!" she told herself, and approached him, and suppressing the terror that gripped her, she pressed her lips to his cheek. But she stepped back at once. All the force of the tenderness she had been feeling for him vanished instantly, replaced by a feeling of horror at what lay before her. "No, he is no more! He is gone, but here where he was is something unfamiliar and hostile, some dreadful, terrifying, repulsive mystery!" And hiding her face in her hands, Princess Mary collapsed into the arms of the doctor, who caught her.

In the presence of Tikhon and the doctor, the women washed what had been the prince, bound up his head with a cloth so the mouth would not stiffen open, and with another cloth tied together the legs that were already spreading apart. Then they dressed him in his uniform with his decorations and placed his shriveled little body on a table. Heaven only knows who arranged all this and when, but it all seemed to happen by itself. Toward evening candles were burning around his coffin, a pall was spread over it, the floor was strewn with sprays of juniper, a printed prayer band was tucked under his shriveled head, and in a corner of the room a chanter sat reading the psalms.

Just as horses shy and snort and crowd around a dead horse, so the members of the household and strangers crowded into the drawing room around the coffin—the Marshal, the village Elder, peasant women—and all with fixed and frightened eyes, crossing themselves, bowed and kissed the old prince's cold and stiffened hand.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Until Prince Andrew settled in Bogucharovo, its owners had always been absentees, and its peasants were quite different in character from those at Bald Hills. They differed in speech, dress, and temperament. They were called steppe peasants. The old prince approved of them for their hard work when they came to Bald Hills to help with the harvest or dig ponds and ditches, but he disliked them for their coarseness.

Prince Andrew's last stay at Bogucharovo, when he introduced hospitals and schools and reduced the rent the peasants had to pay, had not softened their nature but had on the contrary strengthened the very traits the old prince called coarseness. Various obscure rumors always circulated among them: sometimes a rumor that they would all be enrolled as Cossacks; sometimes talk of a new religion everyone would be converted to; then some proclamation of the Tsar's, or an oath to Tsar Paul in 1797 (in connection with which it was rumored that freedom had been granted but the landowners had suppressed it); then tales of Peter Fedorovich's return to the throne in seven years, when everything would be made free and so "simple" that there would be no rules at all. Rumors of the war with Bonaparte and his invasion were linked in their minds with the same vague ideas about the Antichrist, the end of the world, and "pure freedom."

In the area around Bogucharovo there were large villages belonging to the crown or to owners whose serfs paid rent and could work wherever they pleased. There were very few resident landlords nearby and also very few household or literate serfs, and in the lives of the peasantry in those parts, the mysterious undercurrents of Russian popular life—the causes and meaning of which are so baffling to outsiders—were more clearly and strongly evident than elsewhere. One example, which had occurred some twenty years before, was a movement among the peasants to emigrate to some unknown "warm rivers." Hundreds of peasants, including those from Bogucharovo, suddenly began selling their cattle and moving with their entire families toward the southeast. Like birds migrating beyond the sea, these men with their wives and children streamed toward the southeast, to places where none of them had ever been. They set off in caravans, bought their freedom one by one or ran away, and walked or drove toward the "warm rivers." Many were punished, some sent to Siberia, many died of cold and hunger on the road, many returned on their own, and the movement died down by itself just as it had sprung up, without apparent reason. But such undercurrents still existed among the people and gathered new force, ready to manifest themselves just as strangely, unexpectedly, and at the same time simply, naturally, and powerfully. Now in 1812, to anyone living in close contact with these people, it was apparent that these undercurrents were running strong and nearing an eruption.

Alpatych, who had reached Bogucharovo shortly before the old prince's death, noticed an agitation among the peasants, and that contrary to what was happening in the Bald Hills district—where over a radius of forty miles all the peasants were fleeing and leaving their villages to be ransacked by the Cossacks—the peasants in the steppe region around Bogucharovo were, it was rumored, in contact with the French, received leaflets from them that passed from hand to hand, and were not leaving. He learned from loyal household servants that the peasant Karp, who had great influence in the village commune and had recently been away driving a government transport, had returned with news that the Cossacks were destroying abandoned villages, but that the French didn't harm anyone. Alpatych also learned that the day before, another peasant had brought from the village of Visloukhovo, occupied by the French, a proclamation by a French general promising that no harm would come to the inhabitants and that they would be paid for anything taken. As proof, the peasant had brought from Visloukhovo a hundred rubles in banknotes (he didn't know they were counterfeit) paid to him in advance for hay.

More importantly, Alpatych learned that on the very morning he gave the village Elder orders to collect carts to move the princess's luggage from Bogucharovo, a village meeting had been held at which it was decided not to move but to wait. Yet there was no time to waste. On the fifteenth—the day of the old prince's death—the Marshal had insisted that Princess Mary leave immediately, as it was becoming dangerous. He told her that after the sixteenth he couldn't be responsible for what might happen. On the evening of the day the old prince died, the Marshal went away, promising to return the next day for the funeral. But he was unable to do so, because he received word that the French had unexpectedly advanced, and he barely had time to get his own family and possessions away from his estate.
For about thirty years, Bogucharovo had been managed by the village Elder, Dron, whom the old prince called by the pet name "Dronushka."

Dron was one of those physically and mentally vigorous peasants who grow big beards as soon as they come of age and go on unchanged until sixty or seventy, without a gray hair or the loss of a tooth, as straight and strong at sixty as at thirty.

Soon after the migration to the "warm rivers," in which he had taken part like the rest, Dron was made village Elder and overseer of Bogucharovo, and had filled that role irreproachably for twenty-three years. The peasants feared him more than they feared their master. The masters—both the old prince and the young—and the steward respected him and jokingly called him "the Minister." Throughout his entire service, Dron had never been drunk or sick; never, after sleepless nights or the hardest labor, had he shown the slightest fatigue; and though he could not read, he had never forgotten a single money account or the number of sacks of flour in any of the countless cartloads he sold for the prince, nor a single sheaf of the whole grain harvest on any single acre of the Bogucharovo fields.

Alpatych, arriving from the devastated Bald Hills estate, sent for Dron on the day of the prince's funeral and told him to have twelve horses readied for the princess's carriages and eighteen carts for the belongings to be moved from Bogucharovo. Though the peasants paid rent, Alpatych expected no difficulty with this order, since there were two hundred and thirty households at work in Bogucharovo and the peasants were well-off. But on hearing the order, Dron lowered his eyes and said nothing. Alpatych named certain peasants he knew, from whom he told Dron to take the carts.

Dron replied that those peasants' horses were away carting. Alpatych named others, but they too, according to Dron, had no horses available: some were carting for the government, others were too weak, and others had died for lack of fodder. It seemed that no horses could be found even for the carriages, let alone for the carting.

Alpatych looked hard at Dron and frowned. Just as Dron was a model village Elder, so Alpatych had not managed the prince's estates for twenty years in vain. He was a model steward, possessing to the highest degree the ability to read the needs and instincts of those he dealt with. Having glanced at Dron, he immediately understood that the Elder's answers did not reflect his personal views but the general mood of the Bogucharovo commune, which had already carried Dron along with it. But he also knew that Dron, who had acquired property and was hated by the commune, must be torn between two camps: the masters' and the serfs'. He saw this hesitation in Dron's eyes and therefore frowned and stepped closer.

"Now listen, Dronushka," he said. "Don't talk nonsense to me. His excellency Prince Andrew himself gave me orders to move all the people away and not leave them for the enemy, and there's an order from the Tsar about it too. Anyone who stays is a traitor to the Tsar. Do you hear?"
"I hear," Dron answered without lifting his eyes.
Alpatych was not satisfied with this reply.
"Look, Dron, things will end badly!" he said, shaking his head.
"The power is in your hands," Dron replied sadly.

"Listen, Dron, drop this!" Alpatych repeated, withdrawing his hand from his coat front and solemnly pointing to the floor at Dron's feet. "I can see through you—and three yards into the ground under you," he continued, staring at the floor before Dron.
Dron was unsettled, glanced furtively at Alpatych, and lowered his eyes again.

"Drop this nonsense and tell the people to get ready to leave their homes for Moscow, and have carts ready by tomorrow morning for the princess's things. And don't go to any meeting yourself, do you hear?"
Dron suddenly fell to his knees.
"Yakov Alpatych, let me go! Take the keys from me and let me go, for Christ's sake!"

"Stop that!" cried Alpatych sternly. "I see through you and three yards under you," he repeated, knowing that his skill in beekeeping, his knowledge of the right time to sow the oats, and the fact that he had kept the old prince's favor for twenty years had long since earned him a reputation as a wizard, and that the power to see three yards underground is considered an attribute of wizards.
Dron got up and was about to say something, but Alpatych interrupted him.
"What have you all got into your heads, eh?... What are you thinking?"
"What am I supposed to do with the people?" said Dron. "They're completely out of control. I've already told them..."
"'Told them,' I'm sure!" said Alpatych. "Are they drinking?" he asked abruptly.
"Completely out of control, Yakov Alpatych; they've brought in another barrel."
"Well then, listen! I'll go to the police officer, and you tell them so, and that they must stop all this and have the carts ready."
"I understand."

Alpatych did not press further. He had managed people long enough to know that the main way to make them obey is to show no suspicion that they might disobey. Having wrung a submissive "I understand" from Dron, Alpatych left it at that, though he not only doubted but felt almost certain that without military help the carts would not be forthcoming.

And so it was: when evening came, no carts had appeared. In the village, outside the tavern, another meeting was being held, and it was decided to drive the horses into the forest and not provide the carts. Without saying anything about this to the princess, Alpatych had his own belongings taken from the carts that had come from Bald Hills and had those horses harnessed instead for the princess's carriages. Meanwhile he went himself to the police authorities.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: After her father's funeral, Princess Mary shut herself up in her room and refused to see anyone. A maid came to the door to say that Alpatych was asking for orders about their departure. (This was before his talk with Dron.) Princess Mary raised herself from the sofa where she had been lying and replied through the closed door that she didn't intend to go anywhere and asked to be left in peace.

The windows of the room where she lay faced west. She lay on the sofa with her face to the wall, fingering the buttons of the leather cushion and seeing nothing but that cushion, and her confused thoughts centered on one subject—the finality of death and her own spiritual baseness, which she had not suspected but which had revealed itself during her father's illness. She wanted to pray but didn't dare—couldn't, in her present state of mind, address herself to God. She lay there for a long time.

The sun had moved to the other side of the house, and its slanting rays shone through the open window, lighting up the room and part of the leather cushion Princess Mary was looking at. The flow of her thoughts suddenly stopped. Unconsciously she sat up, smoothed her hair, got up, and went to the window, involuntarily breathing in the freshness of the clear but windy evening.
"Yes, you can enjoy the evening now! He's gone and no one will stand in your way," she said to herself, and sinking into a chair, she let her head fall on the windowsill.

Someone spoke her name in a soft and tender voice from the garden and kissed her head. She looked up. It was Mademoiselle Bourienne in a black dress and mourning cap. She softly approached Princess Mary, sighed, kissed her, and immediately began to cry. The princess looked at her. All their former friction and her own jealousy came back to her mind. But she also remembered how he had changed lately toward Mademoiselle Bourienne and could no longer bear the sight of her—showing how unjust the reproaches Princess Mary had mentally leveled at her had been. "Besides, is it for me—I who wished for his death—to condemn anyone?" she thought.

Princess Mary vividly pictured to herself the position of Mademoiselle Bourienne, whom she had recently kept at a distance but who was still dependent on her and living in her house. She felt sorry for her and held out her hand with a look of gentle inquiry. Mademoiselle Bourienne immediately began crying again and kissed that hand, speaking of the princess's sorrow and claiming a share in it. She said her only consolation was that the princess allowed her to share her grief, that all the old misunderstandings should vanish before this great sorrow; that she felt herself blameless toward everyone, and that he, from above, saw her devotion and gratitude. The princess listened, not following the words but occasionally looking up at her and listening to the sound of her voice.

"Your position is doubly terrible, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne after a pause. "I understand that you could not, and cannot, think of yourself, but with my love for you I must do so... Has Alpatych been to you? Has he spoken to you of leaving?" she asked.
Princess Mary did not answer. She didn't understand who was supposed to go or where. "Is it possible to plan or think about anything now? Does anything matter?" she thought, and made no reply.

"You know, dear Marie," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that we are in danger—we are surrounded by the French. It would be dangerous to move now. If we try to go, we will almost certainly be taken prisoner, and God knows..."
Princess Mary looked at her companion without understanding what she was saying.

"Oh, if anyone knew how little anything matters to me now," she said. "Of course I would never want to leave him... Alpatych did say something about going... Speak to him; I can do nothing, nothing, and don't want to..."

"I've spoken to him. He hopes we can still get away tomorrow, but I think it would be better to stay here now," said Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Because, you must agree, dear Marie, to fall into the hands of soldiers or riotous peasants would be terrible."

Mademoiselle Bourienne took from her bag a proclamation (not printed on standard Russian paper) by General Rameau, telling people not to leave their homes and promising that the French authorities would provide proper protection. She handed it to the princess.
"I think it would be best to appeal to that general," she continued. "I'm sure that you would be shown all due respect."
Princess Mary read the paper, and her face began to quiver with stifled sobs.
"Who gave you this?" she asked.
"They probably recognized that I am French, by my name," replied Mademoiselle Bourienne, blushing.
Princess Mary, paper in hand, rose from the window and with a pale face walked out of the room and into what had been Prince Andrew's study.

"Dunyasha! Send Alpatych, or Dronushka, or somebody to me!" she said, "and tell Mademoiselle Bourienne not to come to me," she added, hearing Mademoiselle Bourienne's voice. "We must go at once, at once!" she said, appalled at the thought of being left to the mercy of the French.

"If Prince Andrew found out I was in the power of the French! That I, the daughter of Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky, asked General Rameau for protection and accepted his favor!" This idea horrified her, made her shudder, blush, and feel a surge of anger and pride unlike anything she had ever experienced. All that was distressing, and especially all that was humiliating, in her position rose vividly to her mind. "They, the French, would settle in this house; Monsieur le General Rameau would occupy Prince Andrew's study and amuse himself looking through his letters and papers. Mademoiselle Bourienne would play hostess for him at Bogucharovo. I would be given a small room as a favor; the soldiers would desecrate my father's freshly dug grave to steal his medals and decorations; they would tell me about their victories over the Russians and pretend to sympathize with my grief..." thought Princess Mary, not thinking her own thoughts but feeling compelled to think like her father and brother. For herself she didn't care where she stayed or what happened to her, but she felt herself the representative of her dead father and Prince Andrew. Involuntarily she thought their thoughts and felt their feelings. What they would have said and done, she felt bound to say and do. She went into Prince Andrew's study, trying to enter fully into his way of thinking, and considered her situation.
The demands of life, which had seemed annihilated by her father's death, suddenly rose before her with a new, previously unknown force and took hold of her.

Agitated and flushed, she paced the room, sending now for Michael Ivanovich and now for Tikhon or Dron. Dunyasha, the nurse, and the other maids couldn't say how accurate Mademoiselle Bourienne's claims were. Alpatych was not at home—he had gone to the police. Nor could the architect Michael Ivanovich, who came in with sleepy eyes when sent for, tell Princess Mary anything. With exactly the same smile of agreement with which he had been accustomed to respond to the old prince for fifteen years without expressing opinions of his own, he now answered Princess Mary so that nothing definite could be gathered from his replies. The old valet Tikhon, with his sunken, gaunt face bearing the stamp of inconsolable grief, replied "Yes, Princess" to all her questions and could barely hold back his sobs as he looked at her.
At length Dron, the village Elder, entered the room and with a deep bow to Princess Mary came to a halt by the doorpost.
Princess Mary walked up and down the room and stopped in front of him.

"Dronushka," she said, regarding as a trusted friend this man who always used to bring a special kind of gingerbread from his trips to the Vyazma fair every year and smilingly offer it to her, "Dronushka, now after our misfortune..." she began, but could not go on.
"We are all in God's hands," he said with a sigh.
They were silent for a while.
"Dronushka, Alpatych has gone off somewhere and I have no one to turn to. Is it true, as they tell me, that I can't even leave?"
"Why shouldn't you leave, your excellency? You can go," said Dron.
"I was told it would be dangerous because of the enemy. Dear friend, I can't manage anything. I don't understand anything. I have nobody! I want to go away tonight or early tomorrow morning."
Dron paused. He glanced sideways at Princess Mary and said: "There are no horses; I told Yakov Alpatych so."
"Why are there none?" asked the princess.

"It's all God's punishment," said Dron. "Whatever horses we had were taken for the army or died—it's been that kind of year! We can barely feed ourselves, let alone keep horses. Some go three days without eating. We've got nothing—we've been ruined."
Princess Mary listened carefully to what he told her.
"The peasants are ruined? They have no bread?" she asked.
"They're starving," said Dron. "It's not a matter of carting."
"But why didn't you tell me, Dronushka? Can't something be done to help them? I'll do everything I can..."

To Princess Mary it seemed strange that now, at a moment when such sorrow filled her soul, there could be rich and poor, and that the rich could fail to help the poor. She vaguely knew there was such a thing as "landlord's grain" that was sometimes given to the peasants. She also knew that neither her father nor her brother would refuse to help peasants in need; she only feared making some mistake in distributing the grain she wanted to give. She was glad that such practical concerns presented themselves, allowing her without guilt to forget her own grief. She began asking Dron about the peasants' needs and what belonged to the landlord at Bogucharovo.
"But we have grain belonging to my brother?" she said.
"The landlord's grain is all safe," replied Dron proudly. "Our prince gave no order to sell it."
"Give it to the peasants—let them have everything they need; I give you permission in my brother's name," she said.
Dron said nothing but sighed deeply.
"Give them that grain if there's enough. Distribute it all. I give this order in my brother's name; and tell them that what is ours is theirs. We don't grudge them anything. Tell them that."
Dron looked hard at the princess while she was speaking.
"Let me go, dear lady, for God's sake! Order the keys to be taken from me," he said. "I've served twenty-three years and done no wrong. Let me go, for God's sake!"

Princess Mary didn't understand what he wanted or why he was asking to be discharged. She replied that she had never doubted his devotion and that she was ready to do anything for him and for the peasants.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: An hour later Dunyasha came to tell the princess that Dron had come and all the peasants had gathered at the barn by the princess's order and wished to speak with their mistress.
"But I never told them to come," said Princess Mary. "I only told Dron to give them the grain."
"Only, for God's sake, Princess dear, have them sent away and don't go out to them. It's all a trick," said Dunyasha, "and when Yakov Alpatych comes back, we'll get away... and please don't..."
"What trick?" asked Princess Mary in surprise.
"I just know it is—please listen to me! Ask Nurse too. They say they won't agree to leave Bogucharovo as you ordered."
"You're making some mistake. I never ordered them to leave," said Princess Mary. "Call Dronushka."
Dron came and confirmed Dunyasha's words: the peasants had come by the princess's order.
"But I never sent for them," said the princess. "You must have gotten my message wrong. I only said you should give them the grain."
Dron only sighed in reply.
"If you order it, they will go away," he said.
"No, no. I'll go out to them," said Princess Mary, and despite the protests of the nurse and Dunyasha, she went out to the porch; Dron, Dunyasha, the nurse, and Michael Ivanovich followed her.

"They probably think I'm offering them grain to bribe them into staying here while I myself escape, leaving them to the mercy of the French," thought Princess Mary. "I'll offer them monthly rations and housing on our Moscow estate. I'm sure Andrew would do even more in my place," she thought as she went out in the twilight toward the crowd standing on the pasture by the barn.

The men crowded closer together, stirred, and quickly took off their hats. Princess Mary lowered her eyes and, tripping over her skirt, came right up to them. So many different eyes—old and young—were fixed on her, and there were so many different faces, that she couldn't make out any one of them, and feeling she must address them all at once, she didn't know how. But again the sense that she represented her father and her brother gave her courage, and she bravely began her speech.

"I am very glad you have come," she said without raising her eyes, feeling her heart beating fast and hard. "Dronushka tells me the war has ruined you. That is our shared misfortune, and I will spare nothing to help you. I am leaving because it is dangerous here... the enemy is near... because... I am giving you everything, my friends, and I beg you to take everything—all our grain—so that you won't suffer want! And if you've been told that I'm giving you the grain to keep you here—that is not true. On the contrary, I ask you to go with all your belongings to our estate near Moscow, and I promise you that there you will want for nothing. You will be given food and shelter."
The princess stopped. The only sound from the crowd was sighing.
"I'm not doing this on my own account," she continued. "I do it in the name of my late father, who was a good master to you, and of my brother and his son."
Again she paused. No one broke the silence.
"Ours is a shared misfortune and we will bear it together. Everything that is mine is yours," she concluded, scanning the faces before her.
Every face bore one and the same expression. She couldn't tell whether it was curiosity, devotion, gratitude, or apprehension and distrust—but the expression on all the faces was identical.
"We're very grateful for your kindness, but it won't do for us to take the landlord's grain," said a voice from the back of the crowd.
"But why not?" asked the princess.
No one answered, and Princess Mary, looking around the crowd, found that every eye she met was immediately lowered.
"But why don't you want to take it?" she asked again.
No one answered.
The silence began to oppress the princess and she tried to catch someone's eye.
"Why won't you speak?" she asked a very old man who stood just in front of her, leaning on his stick. "If you think something more is needed, tell me! I'll do anything," she said, catching his eye.
But as if this angered him, he bent his head very low and muttered:
"Why should we agree? We don't want the grain."
"Why should we give up everything? We don't agree. Don't agree... We feel for you, but we're not willing. Go away yourself, alone..." came from various parts of the crowd.
And again all the faces bore the same expression, though now it was certainly not curiosity or gratitude but angry determination.
"But you can't have understood me," said Princess Mary with a sad smile. "Why don't you want to go? I promise to house and feed you, while here the enemy would ruin you..."
But her voice was drowned by the voices of the crowd.
"We won't go! Let them ruin us! We won't take your grain. We don't agree."
Again Princess Mary tried to catch someone's eye, but not a single person in the crowd was looking at her; they were all clearly trying to avoid her gaze. She felt strange and awkward.
"Oh yes, a clever tale! Follow her into slavery! Tear down your houses and go into bondage! Sure! 'I'll give you grain,' she says!" voices in the crowd were heard saying.

With bowed head, Princess Mary left the crowd and went back to the house. Having repeated her order to Dron to have horses ready for her departure the next morning, she went to her room and stayed alone with her thoughts.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: For a long time that night Princess Mary sat by the open window of her room listening to the sound of the peasants' voices reaching her from the village, but she was not thinking about them. She felt she could not understand them no matter how much she thought about them. She thought only of one thing—her sorrow, which, after the interruption caused by present concerns, already seemed to belong to the past. Now she could remember and weep, or pray.

After sunset the wind had dropped. The night was calm and fresh. Toward midnight the voices began to fade, a rooster crowed, the full moon began to show from behind the lime trees, a fresh white dewy mist started to rise, and stillness settled over the village and the house.

Images of the recent past—her father's illness and last moments—rose one after another in her memory. With mournful pleasure she now lingered over these images, pushing away with horror only the last one—the picture of his death—which she felt she could not contemplate, even in imagination, during this still and mystical hour of night. And these images presented themselves to her so clearly and in such detail that they seemed now present, now past, and now future.

She vividly recalled the moment when he had his first stroke and was being dragged by his arms through the garden at Bald Hills, muttering with his helpless tongue, twitching his gray eyebrows, and looking uneasily and timidly at her.

"Even then he wanted to tell me what he told me the day he died," she thought. "He had always thought what he said then." And she recalled in every detail the night at Bald Hills before his last stroke, when with a foreboding of disaster she had stayed home against his wishes. She had not slept and had crept downstairs on tiptoe, and going to the door of the conservatory where he slept that night, she had listened. In a suffering, weary voice he was saying something to Tikhon—speaking of the Crimea and its warm nights and of the Empress. He had obviously wanted to talk. "And why didn't he call me? Why didn't he let me be there instead of Tikhon?" Princess Mary had thought then, and thought again now. "Now he will never tell anyone what was in his soul. Never will that moment return for him or for me when he might have said everything he longed to say, and I—not Tikhon—might have heard and understood. Why didn't I go in?" she thought. "Perhaps he would then have said to me what he said the day he died. While talking to Tikhon he asked about me twice. He wanted to see me, and I was standing right there, outside the door. It was sad and painful for him to talk to Tikhon, who didn't understand. I remember how he began speaking to him about Lise as if she were alive—he had forgotten she was dead—and Tikhon reminded him that she was gone, and he shouted, 'Fool!' He was deeply depressed. From behind the door I heard how he lay down on his bed groaning and cried out, 'My God!' Why didn't I go in then? What could he have done to me? What could I have lost? And perhaps he would have been comforted and would have spoken that word to me." And Princess Mary said aloud the tender word he had spoken on the day of his death. "Dear-est!" she repeated, and began sobbing, with tears that brought relief to her soul. She could now see his face before her. And not the face she had always known and always seen from a distance, but the timid, feeble face she had seen for the first time close up, with all its wrinkles and details, when she stooped near his mouth to catch what he said.
"Dear-est!" she repeated again.

"What was he thinking when he said that word? What is he thinking now?" This question suddenly came to her, and in answer she saw him before her with the expression on his face as he lay in his coffin with his jaw bound up in a white cloth. And the horror that had seized her when she touched him and realized that this was not he but something mysterious and terrible, seized her again. She tried to think of something else and to pray, but could do neither. With wide-open eyes she stared at the moonlight and the shadows, expecting at any moment to see his dead face, and she felt that the silence brooding over the house and within it held her fast.
"Dunyasha," she whispered. "Dunyasha!" she screamed wildly, and tearing herself from that silence she ran to the servants' quarters to meet her old nurse and the maids who came hurrying toward her.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: On the seventeenth of August, Rostov and Ilyin, accompanied by Lavrushka, who had just returned from captivity, and a hussar orderly, left their quarters at Yankovo—ten miles from Bogucharovo—and went for a ride to try out a new horse Ilyin had bought and to find out whether there was any hay to be had in the villages.

For the last three days Bogucharovo had lain between the two hostile armies, so it was as easy for the Russian rearguard to reach it as for the French vanguard. Rostov, as a careful squadron commander, wanted to take whatever provisions remained at Bogucharovo before the French could get them.

Rostov and Ilyin were in the merriest of moods. On the way to Bogucharovo—a princely estate with a manor house and farm where they hoped to find many household servants and pretty girls—they questioned Lavrushka about Napoleon and laughed at his stories, and raced each other to try out Ilyin's horse.
Rostov had no idea that the village he was riding into was the property of that same Bolkonsky who had been engaged to his sister.
Rostov and Ilyin gave their horses free rein for one last race along the slope before reaching Bogucharovo, and Rostov, outpacing Ilyin, was the first to gallop into the village street.
"You're first!" cried Ilyin, flushed.
"Yes, always first—on the grass and here," answered Rostov, stroking his heated Don horse.
"And I'd have won on my Frenchie, your excellency," said Lavrushka from behind, referring to his scruffy cart horse, "only I didn't want to embarrass you."
They rode at a walk to the barn, where a large crowd of peasants stood.

Some of the men bared their heads; others stared at the newcomers without removing their caps. Two tall old peasants with wrinkled faces and thin beards emerged from the tavern, smiling, staggering, and singing some slurred song, and approached the officers.
"Fine fellows!" said Rostov, laughing. "Is there any hay here?"
"And how alike they look," said Ilyin.
"A mo-o-ost me-rr-ry com-pa..." sang one of the peasants with a blissful smile.
One man came out of the crowd and went up to Rostov.
"Who do you belong to?" he asked.
"The French," replied Ilyin jokingly. "And here's Napoleon himself"—and he pointed to Lavrushka.
"So you're Russians?" the peasant asked again.
"And is there a large force of you here?" said another, a short man, coming up.
"Quite large," answered Rostov. "But why have you all gathered here?" he added. "Is it a holiday?"
"The old men have met to discuss village business," replied the peasant, moving away.
At that moment, on the road leading from the manor house, two women and a man in a white hat were seen coming toward the officers.
"The one in pink is mine—hands off!" said Ilyin, spotting Dunyasha running determinedly toward him.
"She'll be ours!" said Lavrushka to Ilyin with a wink.
"What do you want, pretty girl?" said Ilyin with a smile.
"The princess ordered me to ask your regiment and your name."
"This is Count Rostov, squadron commander, and I am your humble servant."
"Co-o-om-pa-ny!" roared the tipsy peasant with a blissful smile, watching Ilyin talk to the girl. Following Dunyasha, Alpatych advanced toward Rostov, having bared his head while still at a distance.

"May I make bold to trouble your honor?" he said respectfully, but with a shade of contempt for the youthfulness of this officer, with one hand inside his coat. "My mistress, the daughter of General-in-Chief Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky, who died on the fifteenth of this month, finding herself in difficulty because of the behavior of these people"—he pointed to the peasants—"asks you to come up to the house... Won't you please ride on a little farther," said Alpatych with a melancholy smile, "as it's not convenient in the presence of..." He indicated the two peasants who hovered near him like horseflies around a horse.
"Ah!... Alpatych... Ah, Yakov Alpatych... Such fun! Forgive us for Christ's sake, eh?" said the peasants, grinning happily at him.
Rostov looked at the tipsy peasants and smiled.
"Or perhaps they amuse your honor?" remarked Alpatych with a straight face, pointing at the old men with his free hand.
"No, there's not much to be amused at here," said Rostov, and rode on a little. "What's the matter?" he asked.

"I must inform your honor that the crude peasants here refuse to let the mistress leave the estate and threaten to unhitch her horses, so that although everything has been packed since this morning, her excellency cannot get away."
"Impossible!" exclaimed Rostov.
"I have the honor of reporting the actual truth," said Alpatych.

Rostov dismounted, gave his horse to the orderly, and followed Alpatych to the house, questioning him about the situation. It turned out that the princess's offer of grain to the peasants the day before, her talk with Dron and at the meeting, had actually had such a bad effect that Dron had finally given up the keys, joined the peasants, and hadn't appeared when Alpatych sent for him; and that in the morning when the princess gave orders to harness for the journey, the peasants had come in a large crowd to the barn and sent word that they would not let her leave the village, that there were orders not to move, and that they would unhitch the horses. Alpatych had gone out to reason with them but was told (it was mainly Karp who did the talking, with Dron staying out of sight) that they couldn't let the princess go, that there was an order against it, but that if she stayed they would serve her as before and obey her in everything.

At the moment when Rostov and Ilyin were galloping down the road, Princess Mary, despite Alpatych's protests, her nurse's warnings, and the maids' pleas, had given orders to harness and intended to leave. But when the cavalrymen were spotted, they were mistaken for Frenchmen; the coachman ran away, and the women in the house began to wail.
"Father! Benefactor! God has sent you!" cried deeply moved voices as Rostov passed through the entrance hall.

Princess Mary was sitting helpless and bewildered in the large sitting room when Rostov was shown in. She couldn't grasp who he was or why he had come, or what was happening to her. When she saw his Russian face, and by his walk and his first words recognized him as a man of her own class, she looked at him with her deep, radiant gaze and began speaking in a voice that faltered and trembled with emotion. To Rostov, this meeting immediately struck him as a romantic event. "A helpless girl, overwhelmed with grief, left to the mercy of coarse, riotous peasants! And what a strange fate sent me here! What gentleness and nobility there are in her features and expression!" he thought as he looked at her and listened to her timid story.

When she began telling him that all this had happened the day after her father's funeral, her voice trembled. She turned away, and then, as if fearing he might take her words as meant to arouse his pity, looked at him with an apprehensive, questioning glance. There were tears in Rostov's eyes. Princess Mary noticed this and looked at him gratefully with that radiant gaze which made the plainness of her face disappear.

"I cannot express, Princess, how glad I am that I happened to ride this way and am able to serve you," said Rostov, rising. "Go whenever you please, and I give you my word of honor that no one shall dare cause you trouble if only you will allow me to act as your escort." And bowing respectfully, as if to a lady of royal blood, he moved toward the door.
Rostov's deferential tone seemed to say that though he would consider himself fortunate to know her, he did not wish to take advantage of her misfortune to impose himself.
Princess Mary understood this and appreciated his delicacy.
"I am very, very grateful to you," she said in French, "but I hope it was all a misunderstanding and that no one is to blame." She suddenly began to cry.
"Excuse me!" she said.
Rostov, with a frown, bowed low again and left the room.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "So, is she pretty? Oh, friend—my pink one is delicious; her name's Dunyasha..."
But glancing at Rostov's face, Ilyin stopped short. He could see that his hero and commander was following an entirely different train of thought.
Rostov glanced angrily at Ilyin and without replying strode rapidly toward the village.
"I'll show them; I'll give it to them, the scoundrels!" he said to himself.
Alpatych, at a gliding trot, just barely managing not to run, kept up with him with difficulty.
"What decision have you been pleased to reach?" he said.
Rostov stopped and, clenching his fists, suddenly turned on Alpatych with fierce intensity.

"Decision? What decision? Old fool!" he cried. "What have you been doing? The peasants are rioting and you can't control them? You're a traitor yourself! I know you. I'll skin you all alive!" And as if afraid of wasting his store of anger, he left Alpatych and strode rapidly forward. Alpatych, mastering his offended feelings, kept pace with Rostov at a gliding gait and continued to share his views. He said the peasants were obstinate and that at this moment it would be unwise to confront them without armed force—wouldn't it be better to send for the military first?
"I'll give them armed force... I'll confront them!" Rostov uttered meaninglessly, breathless with irrational animal fury and the need to vent it.

Without thinking about what he would do, he moved unconsciously with quick, resolute steps toward the crowd. And the closer he got, the more Alpatych felt that this reckless action might actually produce good results. The peasants in the crowd were similarly affected when they saw Rostov's rapid, firm steps and resolute, frowning face.

After the hussars had come to the village and Rostov had gone to see the princess, a certain confusion and division had arisen among the crowd. Some peasants said these newcomers were Russians and might take offense that the mistress was being detained. Dron shared this opinion, but as soon as he expressed it, Karp and others attacked their former Elder.

"How many years have you been fattening off the commune?" Karp shouted at him. "It's all the same to you! You'll dig up your buried pot of money and take it with you... What do you care whether our homes are destroyed or not?"
"We were told to keep order, that nobody's to leave their homes or take a single grain—and that's that!" cried another.

"It was your son's turn to be drafted, but oh no! You were too stingy to part with your big lump of a boy," a little old man suddenly began attacking Dron—"so they took my Vanka and shaved him for a soldier! But we all have to die."
"Sure, we all have to die. I'm not against the commune," said Dron.
"That's right—not against it! You've stuffed your belly..."

The two tall peasants had their say. As soon as Rostov, followed by Ilyin, Lavrushka, and Alpatych, came up to the crowd, Karp, thrusting his fingers into his belt and smiling slightly, moved to the front. Dron, on the contrary, slipped to the rear, and the crowd drew closer together.
"Who's your Elder here? Hey!" shouted Rostov, coming up to the crowd with quick steps.
"The Elder? What do you want with him?" asked Karp.
But before the words were fully out of his mouth, his cap flew off and a fierce blow jerked his head to one side.
"Caps off, traitors!" shouted Rostov furiously. "Where's the Elder?" he demanded.
"The Elder... He wants the Elder!... Dron Zakharych, you!" meek and flustered voices were heard here and there, and caps began to come off.
"We're not rioting, we're following orders," declared Karp, and at that moment several voices began speaking at once.
"It's as the old men decided—there's too many of you giving orders."

"Arguing? Mutiny!... Traitors!" cried Rostov meaninglessly in a voice not his own, gripping Karp by the collar. "Tie him up! Tie him up!" he shouted, though there was no one to do it except Lavrushka and Alpatych.
Lavrushka, however, ran up to Karp and seized his arms from behind.
"Shall I call our men from beyond the hill?" he called out.
Alpatych turned to the peasants and ordered two of them by name to come and bind Karp. The men obediently stepped out of the crowd and began taking off their belts.
"Where's the Elder?" demanded Rostov in a loud voice.
With a pale and frowning face, Dron stepped out of the crowd.
"Are you the Elder? Bind him, Lavrushka!" shouted Rostov, as if that command too could not possibly meet with any resistance.
And in fact two more peasants began tying Dron, who took off his own belt and handed it to them, as if to help.
"And all of you—listen to me!" said Rostov to the peasants. "Get back to your homes at once, and don't let me hear another word out of you!"
"Why, we haven't done anything wrong! We were just being foolish. It's all nonsense... I said at the time it wasn't proper," voices were heard grumbling.
"There! What did I tell you?" said Alpatych, coming into his own again. "It's wrong, boys!"
"All our foolishness, Yakov Alpatych," came the answers, and the crowd immediately began to disperse through the village.
The two bound men were led off to the manor house. The two drunken peasants followed them.
"Aye, look at you!" said one of them to Karp.
"How can you talk to the masters like that? What were you thinking, you fool?" added the other. "A real fool!"

Two hours later the carts stood in the courtyard of the Bogucharovo house. The peasants were briskly carrying out the proprietor's belongings and loading them onto the carts, and Dron, freed at Princess Mary's request from the room where he had been locked up, stood in the yard directing the men.

"Don't just throw it in like that," said one peasant, a man with a round, smiling face, taking a casket from a housemaid. "That cost good money! You can't just chuck it in or shove it under the rope where it'll get scratched. I don't like sloppy work. Let it all be done properly, by the book. Look—put it under the bast matting and cover it with hay—that's the way!"
"Books, books!" said another peasant, carrying out Prince Andrew's bookcases. "Careful—don't bump it! Heavy stuff, boys—solid books."
"Yes, they worked all day and never played!" remarked the tall, round-faced peasant gravely, pointing with a knowing wink at the dictionaries stacked on top.

Not wanting to impose himself on the princess, Rostov didn't return to the house but stayed in the village to wait for her departure. When her carriage drove out, he mounted up and accompanied her eight miles from Bogucharovo to where the road was held by their own troops. At the inn at Yankovo he respectfully took his leave, for the first time allowing himself to kiss her hand.

"How can you say such things!" he said, blushing, in reply to Princess Mary's expressions of gratitude for her rescue, as she called what had happened. "Any policeman would have done the same! If we only had peasants to fight, we wouldn't have let the enemy get this far," he said with a sense of embarrassment and a desire to change the subject. "I'm only glad to have had the chance to meet you. Goodbye, Princess. I wish you happiness and consolation, and hope to see you again in happier circumstances. If you don't want to make me blush, please don't thank me!"

But the princess, even if she didn't thank him again in words, thanked him with her whole expression—her face radiant with gratitude and tenderness. She couldn't believe there was nothing to thank him for. On the contrary, she felt certain that if he hadn't been there, she would have been lost to the mutineers and the French, and that he had exposed himself to terrible and obvious danger to save her. Even more certain was she that he was a man of noble and lofty soul, able to understand her situation and her grief. His kind, honest eyes, with tears rising in them when she herself began to cry as she spoke of her loss, never left her memory.
When she had said goodbye and was alone, she suddenly felt her eyes filling with tears, and then, not for the first time, a strange question presented itself: did she love him?

On the rest of the journey to Moscow, though her situation was not a cheerful one, Dunyasha, who rode with her in the carriage, more than once noticed that her mistress leaned out the window and smiled with an expression of mingled joy and sorrow.
"Well, suppose I do love him?" thought Princess Mary.

Ashamed as she was of admitting to herself that she had fallen in love with a man who might never love her back, she comforted herself with the thought that no one would ever know, and that she would not be to blame if, without ever speaking of it to anyone, she continued to the end of her life to love the man with whom she had fallen in love for the first and last time.

Sometimes when she recalled his looks, his sympathy, and his words, happiness did not seem impossible. It was at those moments that Dunyasha noticed her mistress smiling as she looked out the carriage window.
"Was it not fate that brought him to Bogucharovo, at that very moment?" thought Princess Mary. "And that made his sister refuse my brother?" In all this Princess Mary saw the hand of Providence.

The impression the princess made on Rostov was a very pleasant one. To remember her gave him pleasure, and when his comrades, hearing of his adventure at Bogucharovo, teased him about going to look for hay and instead picking up one of the wealthiest heiresses in Russia, he grew angry. He was angry precisely because the idea of marrying the gentle Princess Mary—who attracted him and had an enormous fortune—had more than once entered his mind against his will. For himself personally, Nicholas could not have wished for a better wife: marrying her would make his mother happy, would set his father's affairs in order, and would even—he felt it—ensure Princess Mary's happiness.
But Sonya? And his promise? That was why Rostov got angry when they teased him about Princess Bolkonskaya.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: On receiving command of the armies, Kutuzov remembered Prince Andrew and sent an order for him to report at headquarters.

Prince Andrew arrived at Tsarevo-Zaimishche on the very day and at the very hour that Kutuzov was reviewing the troops for the first time. He stopped in the village at the priest's house, in front of which stood the commander in chief's carriage, and sat down on a bench at the gate awaiting his Serene Highness, as everyone now called Kutuzov. From the field beyond the village came the sounds of regimental music and then the roar of many voices shouting "Hurrah!" to the new commander in chief. Two orderlies, a courier, and a butler stood nearby, about ten paces from Prince Andrew, taking advantage of Kutuzov's absence and the fine weather. A short, dark lieutenant colonel of hussars with thick mustaches rode up to the gate and, glancing at Prince Andrew, asked whether his Serene Highness was staying there and whether he would be back soon.

Prince Andrew replied that he was not on his Serene Highness's staff but was himself newly arrived. The lieutenant colonel turned to a smart orderly, who, with the particular condescension a commander in chief's orderly shows to officers, replied:
"What? His Serene Highness? He'll probably be here soon. What do you want?"

The lieutenant colonel smiled beneath his mustache at the orderly's tone, dismounted, gave his horse to a dispatch runner, and approached Bolkonsky with a slight bow. Bolkonsky made room for him on the bench and the lieutenant colonel sat down beside him.

"You're also waiting for the commander in chief?" he said. "They say he weceives evewyone, thank God!... It's awful with those sausage eaters! Ermolov had good weason to ask to be pwomoted to German! Now maybe Wussians will get a look in. As it was, devil only knows what was happening. We kept wetweating and wetweating. Did you take part in the campaign?" he asked.

"I had the honor," replied Prince Andrew, "not only of taking part in the retreat but of losing in that retreat everything I held dear—not to mention the estate and birthplace of my family—my father, who died of grief. I belong to the province of Smolensk."

"Ah? You're Pwince Bolkonski? Vewy glad to meet you! I'm Lieutenant Colonel Denisov, better known as Vaska," said Denisov, pressing Prince Andrew's hand and looking into his face with a particularly kind attention. "Yes, I heard about it," he said sympathetically, and after a short pause added: "Yes, it's Scythian warfare. It's all vewy well—only not for those who get it in the neck. So you are Pwince Andwew Bolkonski?" He shook his head. "Vewy pleased, Pwince, to make your acquaintance!" he repeated, smiling sadly, and he pressed Prince Andrew's hand again.

Prince Andrew knew Denisov from what Natasha had told him about her first suitor. This memory carried him sadly and sweetly back to those painful feelings he had not thought about lately but which still lived in his soul. Recently he had received so many new and very serious impressions—the retreat from Smolensk, his visit to Bald Hills, the recent news of his father's death—and had experienced so many emotions, that for a long time those memories had not entered his mind, and now that they did, they did not strike him with nearly their former force. For Denisov too, the memories awakened by the name Bolkonsky belonged to a distant, romantic past, when after supper and Natasha's singing he had proposed to a fifteen-year-old girl without realizing what he was doing. He smiled at the memory of that time and his love for Natasha, and immediately moved on to what now interested him passionately and exclusively. This was a campaign plan he had devised while serving at the outposts during the retreat. He had proposed it to Barclay de Tolly and now wanted to present it to Kutuzov. The plan was based on the fact that the French supply line was too extended, and it proposed that instead of—or alongside—frontal action to block the French advance, we should attack their line of communication. He began explaining his plan to Prince Andrew.
"They can't hold that whole line. It's impossible. I undahtake to bweak thwough. Give me five hundwed men and I'll bweak the line, that's certain! There's only one way—gue-willa warfare!"

Denisov stood up and began gesticulating as he explained his plan to Bolkonsky. In the middle of his explanation, shouts were heard from the army—growing louder, more confused, mingling with music and songs from the field where the review was being held. Hoofbeats and shouts were approaching the village.
"He's coming! He's coming!" shouted a Cossack standing at the gate.

Bolkonsky and Denisov moved to the gate, where a cluster of soldiers forming a guard of honor was standing, and they saw Kutuzov coming down the street mounted on a rather small sorrel horse. A huge suite of generals rode behind him. Barclay was riding almost beside him, and a crowd of officers ran after and around them shouting, "Hurrah!"

His aides galloped into the yard ahead of him. Kutuzov was impatiently urging on his horse, which ambled smoothly under his weight, and he raised his hand to his white Horse Guards cap with its red band and no peak, nodding his head constantly. When he came up to the guard of honor—a fine set of grenadiers mostly wearing decorations—who were saluting him, he looked at them silently and attentively for nearly a minute with the steady gaze of a commander, then turned to the crowd of generals and officers surrounding him. Suddenly his face took on a subtle expression; he shrugged his shoulders as if perplexed.
"And with such fine fellows, to keep retreating and retreating! Well, goodbye, General," he added, and rode into the yard past Prince Andrew and Denisov.
"Hurrah! Hurrah! Hurrah!" shouted those behind him.

Since Prince Andrew had last seen him, Kutuzov had grown still more corpulent, flabby, and fat. But the whitened blind eye, the scar, and the familiar expression of weariness were the same. He wore the white Horse Guards cap and a military overcoat with a whip slung over his shoulder on a thin strap. He sat heavily and swayed limply on his brisk little horse.

"Whew... whew... whew!" he whistled almost inaudibly as he rode into the yard. His face expressed the relief of a man who means to rest after a ceremony. He drew his left foot from the stirrup and, lurching with his whole body and grimacing with the effort, raised it with difficulty onto the saddle, leaned on his knee, groaned, and slid down into the arms of the Cossacks and aides who stood ready to catch him.

He pulled himself together, looked around, squinted, and glanced at Prince Andrew—evidently not recognizing him—and waddled to the porch. "Whew... whew... whew!" he whistled, and again glanced at Prince Andrew. As often happens with old men, it was only after several seconds that the impression of Prince Andrew's face connected with Kutuzov's memory of who he was.
"Ah, how do you do, my dear prince? How do you do, my dear boy? Come along..." he said, glancing wearily around, and he stepped onto the porch, which creaked under his weight.
He unbuttoned his coat and sat down on a bench on the porch.
"And how's your father?"
"I received news of his death yesterday," replied Prince Andrew abruptly.
Kutuzov looked at him with eyes wide open in dismay, then took off his cap and crossed himself:

"May the kingdom of Heaven be his! God's will be done to us all!" He sighed deeply, his whole chest heaving, and was silent for a while. "I loved him and respected him, and I sympathize with you with all my heart."

He embraced Prince Andrew, pressing him to his fat chest, and for some time did not let him go. When he released him, Prince Andrew saw that Kutuzov's flabby lips were trembling and there were tears in his eyes. He sighed and pressed both hands on the bench to raise himself.
"Come! Come with me, we'll talk," he said.

But at that moment Denisov, no more intimidated by his superiors than by the enemy, came up the porch steps with jingling spurs, despite the angry whispers of the aides trying to stop him. Kutuzov, his hands still pressed on the bench, looked at him glumly. Denisov introduced himself and announced that he had something of great importance for the country's welfare to communicate to his Serene Highness. Kutuzov looked wearily at him and, raising his hands with a gesture of annoyance, folded them across his stomach, repeating: "For our country's welfare? Well, what is it? Speak!" Denisov blushed like a girl (it was strange to see the color rise in that shaggy, weathered face) and boldly began to explain his plan for cutting the enemy's supply lines between Smolensk and Vyazma. Denisov came from that region and knew the terrain well. His plan sounded decidedly good, especially delivered with such conviction. Kutuzov looked down at his own legs, occasionally glancing at the door of the adjoining hut as if expecting something unpleasant to come out of it. And from that hut, while Denisov was speaking, a general with a portfolio under his arm really did appear.
"What?" said Kutuzov, interrupting Denisov's explanation. "Ready so soon?"
"Ready, your Serene Highness," replied the general.
Kutuzov shook his head, as if to say: "How is one man supposed to handle it all?" and again listened to Denisov.
"I give my word of honor as a Wussian officer," said Denisov, "that I can bweak Napoleon's line of communication!"
"What relation are you to Intendant General Kiril Andreevich Denisov?" asked Kutuzov, interrupting him.
"He is my uncle, your Sewene Highness."
"Ah, we were friends," said Kutuzov cheerfully. "All right, all right, friend—stay here on the staff and tomorrow we'll talk."
With a nod to Denisov, he turned away and held out his hand for the papers Konovnitsyn had brought him.
"Would your Serene Highness like to come inside?" said the general on duty in a dissatisfied voice. "The plans must be reviewed and several papers signed."
An aide came out and announced that everything was ready inside. But Kutuzov clearly didn't want to enter that room until he was free. He made a face.

"No, have them bring a small table out here, my dear fellow. I'll look at them here," he said. "Don't go," he added, turning to Prince Andrew, who remained on the porch and listened to the general's report.

While this was going on, Prince Andrew heard a woman's voice whispering and the rustle of a silk dress behind the door. Several times, glancing that way, he noticed behind the door a plump, rosy, handsome woman in a pink dress with a lilac silk kerchief on her head, holding a dish and obviously waiting for the commander in chief to enter. Kutuzov's aide whispered to Prince Andrew that this was the wife of the priest whose house it was, and that she intended to offer his Serene Highness bread and salt. "Her husband greeted his Serene Highness with the cross at the church, and she plans to welcome him at home... She's very pretty," the aide added with a smile. At these words Kutuzov glanced around. He was listening to the general's report—which mainly consisted of criticism of the position at Tsarevo-Zaimishche—just as he had listened to Denisov, and just as, seven years before, he had listened to the council of war at Austerlitz. He clearly listened only because he had ears that, though there was a plug of cotton in one of them, couldn't help hearing; but it was plain that nothing the general could say would surprise or even interest him, that he already knew everything that would be said, and heard it only because he had to, as one must sit through a church service. Everything Denisov had said was clever and to the point. What the general was saying was even more clever and to the point. But it was evident that Kutuzov disdained cleverness and knowledge, and knew of something else that would decide matters—something independent of cleverness and knowledge. Prince Andrew watched the commander in chief's face closely, and the only expression he could find there was one of boredom, curiosity about the feminine whispering behind the door, and a desire to maintain decorum. It was clear that Kutuzov disdained cleverness and learning and even the patriotic feeling Denisov had shown, but disdained them not because of his own intellect, feelings, or knowledge—he made no attempt to display any of these—but because of something else. He disdained them because of his old age and his experience of life. The only instruction Kutuzov gave on his own during that report concerned looting by the Russian troops.
