At the end, the general put before him for signature a paper about recovering payments from army commanders for green oats their soldiers had mowed down, in cases where landowners had filed complaints.
After hearing the matter, Kutuzov smacked his lips and shook his head.

"Into the fire with it! I tell you once and for all, my dear fellow," he said, "throw all such things in the fire! Let them cut the crops and burn wood to their hearts' content. I don't order it or allow it, but I don't demand compensation either. You can't get by without it. 'When you chop wood, chips will fly.'" He looked at the paper again. "Oh, this German precision!" he muttered, shaking his head.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: "Well, that's everything!" said Kutuzov as he signed the last document, and rising heavily, smoothing the folds of his fat white neck, he moved toward the door with a more cheerful expression.
The priest's wife, flushing rosy red, picked up the dish she had failed to present at the right moment despite all her preparation, and with a low bow offered it to Kutuzov.
He squinted, smiled, lifted her chin with his hand, and said:
"What a beauty! Thank you, sweetheart!"

He took some gold coins from his trouser pocket and placed them on the dish for her. "Well, my dear, how are we getting on?" he asked, moving to the door of the room assigned to him. The priest's wife smiled, and with dimples in her rosy cheeks, followed him into the room. The aide came out to the porch and asked Prince Andrew to join him for lunch. Half an hour later Prince Andrew was called back to Kutuzov. He found him reclining in an armchair, still in the same unbuttoned overcoat. He had a French book in his hand, which he closed as Prince Andrew entered, marking the place with a knife. Prince Andrew saw by the cover that it was The Knights of the Swan by Madame de Genlis.
"Well, sit down, sit down here. Let's talk," said Kutuzov. "It's sad, very sad. But remember, my dear fellow, that I am like a father to you—a second father..."
Prince Andrew told Kutuzov everything he knew about his father's death, and what he had seen at Bald Hills when he passed through.

"What... what they have brought us to!" Kutuzov suddenly cried in an agitated voice, clearly picturing from Prince Andrew's account the condition Russia was in. "But give me time, give me time!" he said with a grim look, obviously not wishing to continue this upsetting conversation, and added: "I sent for you to keep you with me."
"I thank your Serene Highness, but I'm afraid I'm no longer suited for staff work," replied Prince Andrew with a smile that Kutuzov noticed.
Kutuzov looked at him inquiringly.

"But above all," added Prince Andrew, "I've grown attached to my regiment, I'm fond of the officers, and I believe the men like me too. I would be sorry to leave the regiment. If I decline the honor of being with you, believe me..."
A shrewd, kindly, yet subtly amused expression lit up Kutuzov's fleshy face. He cut Bolkonsky short.

"I'm sorry, because I need you. But you're right, you're right! It's not here that men are needed. There are always plenty of advisers, but not enough men. The regiments wouldn't be what they are if the would-be advisers served in them as you do. I remember you at Austerlitz... I remember, yes, I remember you with the standard!" said Kutuzov, and a flush of pleasure spread over Prince Andrew's face at this memory.

Taking his hand and drawing him down, Kutuzov offered his cheek to be kissed, and again Prince Andrew noticed tears in the old man's eyes. Though Prince Andrew knew Kutuzov's tears came easily, and that he was being especially tender and considerate out of sympathy for his loss, this reminder of Austerlitz was both pleasant and flattering.

"Go your way and God be with you. I know your path is the path of honor!" He paused. "I missed you at Bucharest, but I needed someone to send." And changing the subject, Kutuzov began to speak of the Turkish war and the peace that had been concluded. "Yes, I was much criticized," he said, "both for that war and the peace... but everything came at the right time. Everything comes to him who knows how to wait. And there were just as many advisers there as here..." he went on, returning to the topic of "advisers" that clearly preoccupied him. "Ah, those advisers!" he said. "If we had listened to them all, we'd never have made peace with Turkey and would never have finished that war. Everything in haste, but the more haste, the less speed. Kamensky would have been ruined if he hadn't died. He stormed fortresses with thirty thousand men. It's not hard to capture a fortress, but it's hard to win a campaign. For that, you don't need storming and attacking—you need patience and time. Kamensky sent soldiers against Rushchuk, but I used only those two things—patience and time—and I took more fortresses than Kamensky, and made the Turks eat horseflesh!" He swayed his head. "And the French will too, believe me," he went on, growing more animated and striking his chest, "I'll make them eat horseflesh!" And tears again dimmed his eyes.
* "Everything comes in time to him who knows how to wait."
"But won't we have to accept battle?" asked Prince Andrew.

"We will if everyone wants it; it can't be helped... But believe me, my dear boy, there is nothing stronger than those two: patience and time—they will do everything. But the advisers don't see it that way, and that's the trouble. Some want one thing, others want something else. What's one to do?" he asked, evidently expecting an answer. "Well, what do you want us to do?" he repeated, and his eye shone with a deep, shrewd look. "I'll tell you what to do," he continued, since Prince Andrew still didn't reply: "I'll tell you what to do, and what I do. When in doubt, my dear fellow"—he paused—"do nothing." He articulated the French proverb deliberately.
* "Don't see it that way—that's the trouble."
* "When in doubt, my dear fellow, do nothing."

"Well, goodbye, my dear fellow; remember that with all my heart I share your sorrow, and that for you I am not a Serene Highness, nor a prince, nor a commander in chief, but a father! If you need anything, come straight to me. Goodbye, my dear boy."
Again he embraced and kissed Prince Andrew, but before the latter had left the room Kutuzov gave a sigh of relief and went back to his unfinished novel, The Knights of the Swan by Madame de Genlis.

Prince Andrew could not have explained how or why, but after that interview with Kutuzov he returned to his regiment reassured about the general course of affairs and about the man to whom they had been entrusted. The more he recognized the absence of all personal ambition in the old man—in whom there seemed to remain only the habit of old passions, and in place of an intellect that groups events and draws conclusions, only the ability to calmly observe the course of events—the more reassured he was that everything would be as it should. "He won't introduce any plan of his own. He won't devise or initiate anything," thought Prince Andrew, "but he will listen to everything, remember everything, and put everything in its proper place. He will not obstruct anything useful or permit anything harmful. He understands that there is something stronger and more important than his own will—the inevitable course of events—and he can see them and grasp their significance, and seeing that significance, can refrain from meddling and renounce his personal desires. And above all," thought Prince Andrew, "one believes in him because he's Russian, despite the novel by Genlis and the French proverbs, and because his voice shook when he said: 'What they have brought us to!' and there was a sob in it when he said he would 'make them eat horseflesh!'"

On such feelings—more or less dimly shared by all—were founded the unanimity and general approval with which, despite the court's influence, Kutuzov's popular appointment as commander in chief was received.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After the Emperor left Moscow, life flowed on there in its usual course, and that course was so ordinary that it was hard to remember the recent days of patriotic fervor, hard to believe that Russia was really in danger and that the members of the English Club were also sons of the Fatherland, ready to sacrifice everything for it. The one thing that recalled the patriotic enthusiasm everyone had shown during the Emperor's stay was the call for contributions of men and money—a demand that, once the promises had been made, assumed a legal, official form and became unavoidable.

With the enemy's approach to Moscow, the Muscovites' view of their situation did not grow more serious but actually became more frivolous, as always happens with people who see a great danger approaching. At the approach of danger, two voices always speak with equal power in the human soul: one very reasonably tells a person to consider the nature of the danger and the means of escaping it; the other, still more reasonably, says that it is too depressing and painful to think about the danger since it is not in our power to foresee everything and avert the general course of events, and that it is therefore better to ignore what is painful until it arrives, and to think about what is pleasant. In solitude, a person generally listens to the first voice; in society, to the second. So it was now with the people of Moscow. It had been a long time since people had been as merry in Moscow as that year.

Rostopchin's broadsheets, headed by woodcuts of a tavern, a barkeeper, and a Moscow citizen named Karpushka Chigirin "who—having been a militiaman and having had a bit too much at the pub—heard that Napoleon wanted to come to Moscow, got angry, cursed the French in terrible language, came out of the tavern, and under the sign of the eagle began to address the crowd" were read and discussed, alongside the latest witty verses by Vasili Lvovich Pushkin.

In the Club's corner room, members gathered to read these broadsheets, and some enjoyed the way Karpushka mocked the French, saying: "They'll swell up on Russian cabbage, burst on our buckwheat porridge, and choke on cabbage soup. They're all dwarfs, and one peasant woman could toss three of them with a pitchfork." Others disliked the tone and called it stupid and vulgar. It was said that Rostopchin had expelled all Frenchmen and even all foreigners from Moscow, and that there had been spies and agents of Napoleon among them; but this was mainly told so as to introduce Rostopchin's witty remark on the occasion. The foreigners were deported to Nizhni by boat, and Rostopchin had told them in French: "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and don't turn it into the boat of Charon." There was talk of all the government offices having already been moved from Moscow, and to this Shinshin's quip was added—that for that alone, Moscow ought to be grateful to Napoleon. It was said that Mamonov's regiment would cost him eight hundred thousand rubles, and that Bezukhov had spent even more on his, but that the best thing about Bezukhov's gesture was that he himself was going to put on a uniform and ride at the head of his regiment without charging anything for the show.
* "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and take care not to make it the boat of Charon."
"You don't spare anyone," said Julie Drubetskaya as she gathered and pressed together a bunch of shredded lint with her thin, ringed fingers.
Julie was preparing to leave Moscow the next day and was hosting a farewell party.
"Bezukhov is ridiculous, but he is so kind and good-natured. What pleasure is there in being so caustic?"
"A forfeit!" cried a young man in militia uniform whom Julie called "my knight" and who was traveling with her to Nizhni.

In Julie's circle, as in many other circles in Moscow, it had been agreed that they would speak nothing but Russian, and anyone who slipped into French would pay a fine to the Committee of Voluntary Contributions.
"Another forfeit for a Gallicism," said a Russian writer who was present. "'What pleasure is there in being' is not Russian!"
"You don't spare anyone," Julie continued to the young man, ignoring the writer's remark.

"For 'caustic'—I'm guilty and I'll pay, and I'm prepared to pay again for the pleasure of telling you the truth. For Gallicisms I won't take responsibility," she said, turning to the writer. "I have neither the money nor the time, like Prince Galitsyn, to hire a tutor to teach me Russian!"

"Ah, here he is!" she added. "When one— No, no," she said to the militia officer, "you won't catch me. Speak of the sun and you see its rays!" and she smiled charmingly at Pierre. "We were just talking about you," she said with the easy dishonesty natural to a society woman. "We were saying your regiment would certainly be better than Mamonov's."
"Oh, don't talk to me about my regiment," replied Pierre, kissing his hostess's hand and taking a seat beside her. "I'm so sick of it."
"You will, of course, command it yourself?" said Julie, directing a sly, sarcastic glance at the militia officer.

The latter, in Pierre's presence, had stopped being sarcastic, and his face expressed confusion about what Julie's smile might mean. Despite his absentmindedness and good nature, Pierre's personality immediately checked any attempt to ridicule him to his face.
"No," said Pierre, with a laughing glance at his large, stout body. "I'd make too easy a target for the French. Besides, I doubt I could even climb onto a horse."
Among the people Julie's guests happened to gossip about were the Rostovs.

"I hear their affairs are in very bad shape," said Julie. "And he is so unreasonable, the count himself, I mean. The Razumovskis wanted to buy his house and his estate near Moscow, but it just drags on and on. He asks too much."
"No, I think the sale will go through in a few days," said someone. "Though it's madness to buy anything in Moscow now."
"Why?" asked Julie. "You don't think Moscow is in danger?"
"Then why are you leaving?"
"Me? What a question! I'm leaving because... well, because everyone is leaving; and besides, I'm not Joan of Arc or an Amazon."
"Well, of course, of course! Let me have some more strips of linen."
"If he manages the business properly, he should be able to pay off all his debts," said the militia officer, speaking of Rostov.

"A kindly old man but not very capable. And why are they staying on so long in Moscow? They meant to leave for the country ages ago. Natalie is quite well again now, isn't she?" Julie asked Pierre with a knowing smile.

"They're waiting for their younger son," Pierre replied. "He joined Obolensky's Cossacks and was sent to Belaya Tserkov where the regiment is being formed. But now they've had him transferred to my regiment and they're expecting him any day. The count wanted to leave long ago, but the countess absolutely won't leave Moscow until her son arrives."
"I saw them the day before yesterday at the Arkharovs'. Natalie has gotten her looks back and is more cheerful. She sang a song. How easily some people get over things!"
"Get over what?" asked Pierre, looking displeased.
Julie smiled.
"You know, Count, knights like you are only found in Madame de Souza's novels."
"What knights? What do you mean?" demanded Pierre, blushing.
"Oh, come, my dear count! It's the talk of all Moscow. I admire you, I truly do!"
* "It's the talk of all Moscow. My word, I admire you!"
"Forfeit, forfeit!" cried the militia officer.
"All right, one can't say anything—how tiresome!"
"What is 'the talk of all Moscow'?" Pierre asked angrily, rising to his feet.
"Come now, Count, you know!"
"I don't know anything about it," said Pierre.
"I know you were friends with Natalie, and so... but I was always closer to Vera—that dear Vera."

"No, madame!" Pierre continued in a tone of displeasure. "I have not taken on the role of Natalie Rostova's knight at all, and haven't visited them for nearly a month. But I cannot understand the cruelty..."

"He who excuses himself, accuses himself," said Julie, smiling and waving the lint triumphantly, and to have the last word she quickly changed the subject. "Do you know what I heard today? Poor Mary Bolkonskaya arrived in Moscow yesterday. Did you know she lost her father?"
* "He who excuses himself, accuses himself."
"Really? Where is she? I would very much like to see her," said Pierre.
"I spent the evening with her yesterday. She's going to their estate near Moscow either today or tomorrow morning, with her nephew."
"Well, how is she?" asked Pierre.

"She's all right, but sad. But do you know who rescued her? It's quite a romance. Nicholas Rostov! She was surrounded, they wanted to kill her and had wounded some of her people. He rushed in and saved her..."
"Another romance," said the militia officer. "Really, this general exodus has been arranged to get all the old maids married off. Catiche is one and Princess Bolkonskaya another."
"Do you know, I actually think she's a tiny bit in love with the young man."
* "A little bit in love with the young man."
"Forfeit, forfeit, forfeit!"
"But how would you say that in Russian?"

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: When Pierre returned home, he was handed two of Rostopchin's broadsheets that had been delivered that day.

The first declared that the report of Count Rostopchin forbidding people to leave Moscow was false; on the contrary, he was glad that ladies and merchants' wives were leaving the city. "There will be less panic and less gossip," the broadsheet read, "but I will stake my life that that scoundrel will not enter Moscow." These words showed Pierre clearly, for the first time, that the French would enter Moscow. The second broadsheet stated that Russian headquarters were at Vyazma, that Count Wittgenstein had defeated the French, but that since many Moscow residents wished to be armed, weapons were available at the arsenal: sabers, pistols, and muskets at a low price. The tone of the proclamation was not as playful as the earlier Chigirin bulletins. Pierre pondered these broadsheets. Clearly, the terrible storm he had longed for with his whole soul—yet which filled him with involuntary dread—was drawing near.
"Should I join the army and enlist, or wait?" he asked himself for the hundredth time. He took a pack of cards from the table and began laying them out for a game of patience.
"If this patience works out," he said to himself after shuffling the cards, holding them in his hand and looking up, "if it works out, it means... what does it mean?"
He hadn't decided what it would mean when he heard the eldest princess's voice at the door, asking whether she might come in.
"Then it will mean I must go to the army," Pierre said to himself. "Come in, come in!" he called to the princess.
Only the eldest princess—the one with the stony face and long waist—was still living in Pierre's house. The two younger ones had both married.

"Excuse me for disturbing you, cousin," she said in a reproachful, agitated voice. "But you know some decision must be made. What is going to happen? Everyone has left Moscow and the people are rioting. Why are we still here?"
"On the contrary, everything seems satisfactory, dear cousin," said Pierre in the bantering tone he habitually used with her, always feeling uncomfortable in the role of her benefactor.

"Satisfactory? Very satisfactory! Barbara Ivanovna was telling me today how our troops are distinguishing themselves. That is certainly to their credit! And the people too are getting quite unruly—even my maid has started being rude. At this rate they'll soon be beating us. One can't walk in the streets. But above all, the French will be here any day now, so what are we waiting for? I ask just one thing of you, cousin," she went on, "arrange for me to be taken to Petersburg. Whatever I may be, I can't live under Bonaparte's rule."
"Oh come, dear cousin! Where do you get your information? On the contrary..."
"I won't submit to your Napoleon! Others can if they wish... If you don't want to do this..."
"But I will, I'll arrange it right away."
The princess was clearly annoyed at having no one to be angry with. Muttering to herself, she sat down in a chair.

"But you've been misinformed," said Pierre. "Everything is quiet in the city and there's not the slightest danger. See—I was just reading..." He showed her the broadsheet. "Count Rostopchin writes that he'll stake his life that the enemy won't enter Moscow."

"Oh, that count of yours!" said the princess spitefully. "He's a hypocrite, a scoundrel who stirred up the people to riot himself. Didn't he write in those idiotic broadsheets that anyone, 'whoever it might be, should be dragged to the lockup by his hair'? How silly! 'And honor and glory to whoever catches him,' he says. That's what his flattery has led to! Barbara Ivanovna told me the crowd nearly killed her because she said something in French."
"Oh, but that's so... You take everything too much to heart," said Pierre, and began laying out his cards for patience.

Although the patience did come out, Pierre did not join the army but remained in the deserted city, still in the same state of agitation, indecision, and anxiety, yet at the same time joyfully awaiting something terrible.

The next day toward evening, the princess departed, and Pierre's chief steward came to inform him that the money needed to equip his regiment could not be found without selling one of the estates. The steward's general message was that Pierre's project of raising a regiment would ruin him. Pierre listened, barely suppressing a smile.
"Well then, sell it," he said. "What's to be done? I can't back out now!"

The worse everything became—especially his own affairs—the more pleased Pierre was, and the more evident it seemed that the catastrophe he expected was approaching. Almost no one he knew was left in town. Julie had gone, and Princess Mary too. Of his close friends, only the Rostovs remained, but he didn't go to see them.

To distract himself, he drove that day to the village of Vorontsovo to see the great balloon Leppich was building to destroy the enemy, and a trial balloon that was to go up the next day. The balloon wasn't ready yet, but Pierre learned it was being built by the Emperor's order. The Emperor had written to Count Rostopchin as follows:
As soon as Leppich is ready, assemble a crew of reliable and intelligent men for his gondola and send a courier to General Kutuzov to inform him. I have already told him about it.

Please impress upon Leppich that he must be very careful where he makes his first descent, so he doesn't make a mistake and fall into enemy hands. It is essential that he coordinate his movements with the commander in chief.

On his way home from Vorontsovo, passing through Bolotnaya Square, Pierre saw a large crowd around the Lobnoe Place and stopped to get out of his carriage. A French cook accused of being a spy was being flogged. The flogging had just ended, and the executioner was releasing from the flogging bench a stout man with red whiskers, wearing blue stockings and a green jacket, who was moaning piteously. Another man, thin and pale, stood nearby. Judging by their faces, both were French. With a frightened, suffering expression like the one on the thin Frenchman's face, Pierre pushed his way through the crowd.
"What is it? Who is it? What's it for?" he kept asking.

But the crowd—officials, townspeople, shopkeepers, peasants, and women in shawls and fur coats—was so absorbed in what was happening at the Lobnoe Place that no one answered him. The stout man got up, frowned, shrugged his shoulders, and clearly trying to look composed, began pulling on his jacket without looking around; but suddenly his lips trembled and he began to cry, the way full-blooded grown men cry, angry with themselves for doing so. People in the crowd began talking loudly, apparently to drown out their own feelings of pity, or so it seemed to Pierre.
"He's the cook to some prince."
"Well now, mister, seems Russian sauce is a bit sour for a Frenchman... sets his teeth on edge!" said a wrinkled clerk standing behind Pierre, as the Frenchman began to cry.
The clerk looked around, obviously hoping his joke would be appreciated. Some people laughed; others continued to watch in dismay as the executioner was undressing the other man.

Pierre choked, his face contorted, and he turned hastily away, went back to his carriage muttering something to himself, and climbed in. As they drove, he shuddered and cried out several times so loudly that the coachman asked:
"What is your pleasure?"
"Where are you going?" shouted Pierre to the coachman, who was heading toward Lubyanka Street.
"To the Governor's, as you ordered," answered the coachman.
"Fool! Idiot!" shouted Pierre, abusing his coachman—something he rarely did. "Home, I told you! And drive faster, you blockhead!" "I must get away this very day," he muttered to himself.

The sight of the tortured Frenchman and the crowd around the Lobnoe Place had so firmly decided Pierre that he could no longer stay in Moscow and would leave for the army that very day, that it seemed either he had already told the coachman this or that the man should have known it on his own.

On reaching home, Pierre told Evstafey—his head coachman, who knew everything, could do anything, and was known to all Moscow—that he would leave that night for the army at Mozhaysk, and ordered him to send his saddle horses ahead. This couldn't all be arranged that day, so on Evstafey's advice Pierre had to postpone his departure until the next day to allow time for the relay horses to go on ahead.

On the twenty-fourth, the weather cleared after a spell of rain, and after dinner Pierre left Moscow. When changing horses that night at Perkhushkovo, he learned that there had been a great battle that evening. (This was the battle of Shevardino.) He was told that there in Perkhushkovo the earth trembled from the gunfire, but nobody could answer his questions about who had won. At dawn the next day Pierre was approaching Mozhaysk.
Every house in Mozhaysk had soldiers quartered in it, and at the inn where Pierre was met by his groom and coachman there was no room to be had. It was full of officers.

Everywhere in Mozhaysk and beyond it, troops were stationed or on the march. Cossacks, infantry, cavalry, wagons, ammunition carts, and cannons were everywhere. Pierre pushed forward as fast as he could, and the farther he left Moscow behind and the deeper he plunged into that sea of troops, the more he was overcome by restless excitement and a new, joyful feeling he had never experienced before. It was a feeling similar to what he had felt at the Sloboda Palace during the Emperor's visit—a sense that he must undertake something and sacrifice something. He now experienced a glad awareness that everything that makes up human happiness—the comforts of life, wealth, even life itself—is rubbish that it is pleasant to throw away, compared with something... With what? Pierre could not say, and he didn't try to determine for whom or for what he felt such particular joy in sacrificing everything. He wasn't concerned with the question of what to sacrifice for; the very act of sacrificing brought him a new and joyful sensation.
